power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 1.000", "p = 0.094", "p = 0.068", "p = 0.71", "p = 0.100"), Sentence = c("After completion of the arch, ΔTTP returned to baseline (P8-P10: -0.1, +1.0 and +0.1 s; Holm-adjusted p = 1.000).", "The interhemispheric rSO 2 difference (right -left), analysed with the same model, differed from baseline only nominally under unilateral SACP (P3; +5.4 percentage points, 1.3 to 9.6; unadjusted p = 0.010), and no contrast survived Holm correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.094; Supplementary Results).", "Within the configurations in which the arch vessels change between selective and body perfusion (P4-P8), excluding the circulatory states before SACP and during rewarming, rSO 2 nevertheless fell with increasing TTP: by -0.24 percentage points per second on the left (95% CI -0.40 to -0.08; p = 0.004) and by -0.21 on the right, where it is reported as a trend (-0.43 to +0.02; p = 0.068), without a difference between hemispheres (interaction p = 0.71; Fig. 3B).", "Within the configurations in which the arch vessels change between selective and body perfusion (P4-P8), excluding the circulatory states before SACP and during rewarming, rSO 2 nevertheless fell with increasing TTP: by -0.24 percentage points per second on the left (95% CI -0.40 to -0.08; p = 0.004) and by -0.21 on the right, where it is reported as a trend (-0.43 to +0.02; p = 0.068), without a difference between hemispheres (interaction p = 0.71; Fig. 3B).", "In contrast, the three patients without cerebral injury ranked fourth to sixth on both the adjusted and raw scales (exact Wilcoxon p = 0.100, the smallest value attainable with three patients per group; Fig. 3A)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Ten adults undergoing aortic arch surgery with SACP were enrolled when the measurement team and equipment were available: nine for FET repair and one for hemiarch replacement (Table 1; full characteristics in Table S1).
